opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, because the word has been stretched to cover almost anything with a chatbot interface and a "do it for me" button. But I don't think the hype means there's nothing there. The way I'd put it is that "agent" isn't a single thing; it's a spectrum, and the term is useful as long as we're clear about which dimension we're talking about.

At one end, you have a language model that just answers a question. As you move along the spectrum, systems take on more of a few properties: they operate in more complex, open-ended environments; they pursue goals with less direct supervision; they can take actions in the world, like calling tools, browsing, writing and running code, sending emails; and they plan over multiple steps rather than producing one response. The more of those a system has, the more "agentic" it is. That framing is meaningful because those properties genuinely change how we should think about evaluation, reliability, and risk.

Take evaluation. With a chatbot, you can more or less judge the output in isolation. With an agent, the cost of the system matters, because you can always throw more retries or more compute at a task and boost accuracy on a benchmark. So if you don't measure cost alongside accuracy, you get leaderboards that tell you very little about real-world usefulness. Benchmarks also get overfit in ways that are easier to miss when the agent is doing a long chain of actions. Those problems are specific to agents, so having a word for the category actually helps us notice them.

And reliability matters much more once a system acts on your behalf. A model that's right 90% of the time is fine for brainstorming, but an agent booking travel or touching your finances that fails one time in ten is basically unusable. That gap between capability and reliability is, I think, the central challenge, and it's why a lot of the flashy demos haven't turned into products people trust.

So my view is: be skeptical of the marketing, but don't throw out the concept. "Agent" points to a real shift in what these systems do, and that shift brings real new questions that the field needs to take seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes agentic systems as taking actions, pursuing goals, and planning over multiple steps, but it does not argue that scaling alone cannot achieve AI or that usefulness beyond zero-shot prompting requires more complex scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It calls “agent” a useful term for a spectrum of system behaviors and properties, but does not ground its meaning in naming compound AI systems built around models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot of justified cynicism about the word "agents" right now, because it's being applied to everything from a chatbot with a slightly longer system prompt to these sci-fi visions of fully autonomous systems running companies. And when a term is stretched that far, it's tempting to say it means nothing.

But I actually don't think that's right. When we looked at this carefully, what we found is that "agent" isn't a binary category, it's more of a spectrum, and the dimensions of that spectrum are pretty meaningful. One is how complex the environment and the goals are. A system that completes a single turn of a conversation is very different from one that's pursuing a multi-step objective over a long horizon in an open-ended environment like the web. A second dimension is how much autonomy the system has, how often a human is in the loop, whether the system is taking actions that have real consequences in the world rather than just producing text for a person to read. And a third is the system design itself, things like planning, tool use, having some memory, reflecting on and correcting its own mistakes.

So if you think of agentic-ness as the degree to which a system sits further along those dimensions, then the term is actually doing real work. It's pointing at a genuine shift from models that you ask a question and get an answer, to systems that you delegate a task to and that go off and do things. That shift matters enormously for how we evaluate these systems, because accuracy on a benchmark isn't the point anymore, it's reliability over many steps and cost and safety. And it matters for the societal implications, because once a system is acting rather than just talking, the failure modes look very different.

So my view is: resist the hype, be very skeptical of specific product claims, but don't throw out the concept. The concept is capturing something real, and we're going to need the vocabulary to talk about it carefully.

r001.rationale: The response describes agent dimensions such as multi-step goals, autonomy, tool use, and memory, but does not argue that scaling alone cannot achieve AI or that greater usefulness than zero-shot prompting requires more complex scaffolding.

r002.rationale: It says “agents” captures a real shift toward systems that act and delegate tasks, but does not ground the term’s meaning in naming compound AI systems built around models.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a useful distinction underneath the hype. With a chatbot, you ask a question, it gives you an answer, and you decide what to do with it. With an agent, you give it a goal, and it can take actions toward that goal—use tools, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. You’re delegating some control over the process, rather than just asking it to generate text.

That’s meaningful because it changes how we need to think about reliability. If a chatbot gives you a bad answer, you have an opportunity to catch it before acting. If an agent makes a mistake and then takes further actions based on that mistake, the consequences can compound. So we need to ask what it’s allowed to do, when it should ask for help, and how we can tell whether it accomplished the task.

Of course, that doesn’t make “agent” a precise, binary category. Systems can have different degrees of autonomy, and calling something an agent doesn’t establish that it works well. But the underlying shift—from generating answers to taking actions—is real enough to deserve a term.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses agents taking actions and reliability, but does not argue that scaling models alone is insufficient or that greater usefulness requires more complex scaffolding.

r002.rationale: The candidate grounds “agents” in the shift from generating answers to taking actions, but does not say the term names compound AI systems built around models.

I think there’s a useful distinction underneath the hype. With a chatbot, you ask a question and it gives you a response. With an agent, you give it a goal, and it can take actions toward that goal—use tools, observe what happens, and decide what to do next. So you’re delegating some control over a process, rather than just asking for a piece of text.

Now, that’s a spectrum. There isn’t a sharp boundary where something suddenly becomes an agent. And calling a system an agent doesn’t tell you whether it can do any of those things reliably. But the distinction matters because once a system can act, we have to ask different questions: What permissions does it have? When should it ask for human approval? How do we catch mistakes before they compound? Those are real engineering questions, even if the marketing gets ahead of the capabilities.
